entities.summary:
David Anhaght, also known as David the Invincible or David the Philosopher, was a preeminent Neoplatonist philosopher of the 6th century CE, whose intellectual contributions profoundly shaped the philosophical and theological landscape of late antique Armenia. Born in Armenia, he is traditionally believed to have studied in the vibrant intellectual centers of Alexandria and Athens, becoming a master of Aristotelian logic and Neoplatonic metaphysics. His significance lies in his role as a crucial conduit for transmitting and adapting classical Greek thought into the burgeoning Armenian intellectual tradition, bridging pagan philosophical rigor with early Christian scholasticism.

His principal works, primarily written in Greek and subsequently translated into Armenian, include the foundational 'Definitions of Philosophy' and extensive commentaries on Aristotle's 'Categories' and Porphyry's 'Isagoge'. These texts systematically introduced and elucidated complex concepts of logic, epistemology, and ontology, making them accessible and applicable within an Armenian Christian context. David's meticulous analysis and synthesis of these classical sources provided a robust framework for theological discourse and education, distinguishing him as a pivotal figure in the development of Armenian intellectual history.

David Anhaght's philosophical system became a cornerstone of Armenian monastic and cathedral schools for centuries, establishing a curriculum grounded in rigorous logical inquiry and metaphysical speculation. His influence extended far beyond his lifetime, shaping later Armenian thinkers and ensuring the preservation and transmission of significant portions of ancient Greek philosophy to the medieval East. He is considered a foundational figure in the Armenian intellectual renaissance of the 7th and 8th centuries, with his methods and interpretations permeating subsequent scholarly works.
